title: Prophecy needs preparation
hookLine: prophecy requires mind, character and imagination
last: GOD HAS NO BODY; THE HAND MEANS ACTING.

cards: Three kings and their armies are stuck in a desert with no water, and they come to the prophet Elisha for a word from God. He has hard words for one of them, the king of Israel. Then he asks for something odd.
Not a scroll, not an altar. A musician. "But now bring me a minstrel."
The musician plays, and the text says the hand of the LORD came upon him, and he speaks. Why would a prophet need music first? Maimonides has an answer.

teach.b: Prophecy needs preparation. First, the mind.
In his law code, Maimonides writes that prophecy rests only on a person great in wisdom, strong in character, whose impulses never overpower them.
The Guide explains why: prophecy flows from God first into a person's reasoning mind, and a mind that hasn't been trained has nowhere to hold it. Second, character.
A person ruled by appetite, by greed, by the hunger for honor, is pulled too many ways to receive anything. So the work on character from his Eight Chapters, the middle way, isn't a separate subject.
It's part of the same preparation.
Third, imagination, the surprising one. Prophecy then flows into the imagination, he says, which is why prophets see visions, parables and dreams, not lectures.
A philosopher with a strong mind but a weak imagination might understand deeply and still not be a prophet. And imagination is fragile: sadness and anger shut it down.
That's how he reads Elisha: angered, he needed the music to bring back joy and calm before prophecy could come. Fourth, the limit. Does all this preparation guarantee prophecy?
No. Even a fully prepared person may not receive it, Maimonides holds, if God withholds it. Preparation doesn't force the gift.
It makes a person able to hold it.
For him, that's the line between a vessel and a demand.

how: Jews who study Maimonides read his account of prophecy in the Laws of the Foundations of the Torah, chapter seven, and in the second part of the Guide. Tradition holds that prophecy has ceased, so the teaching is studied as a picture of human readiness.

o: a prophet's fast before giving a public speech
a ready mind, character and imagination, before prophecy
the training of musicians who played in the Temple

games.q: prophecy needs preparation — tap the pairs.

s: for Maimonides, anyone fully prepared is guaranteed prophecy
he holds that God may still withhold it. preparation makes a person able, not entitled.
Maimonides gives the imagination a role in prophecy
prophecy flows into the imagination too, which is why prophets see visions and parables.
Elisha prophesied right away, straight after his hard words
he asked for a minstrel first. Maimonides reads it as music restoring calm and joy after anger.

games.q: you're Elisha. three kings want a word from God, and you've just spoken hard words to one of them. what do you do?
o: speak at once, angry or not.
ask for a musician to play first.
games.why: he says, 'but now bring me a minstrel.' when the music plays, the hand of the LORD comes upon him.

practice: Check in on the three things Maimonides names: is your mind rested or scattered, is your character pulled by irritation, wanting or worry, is there room in you for a picture or a song?
Pick the one that needs the most care, and let one small kindness toward it come to mind: a page of real reading, a grudge set down, or a piece of music, the way Elisha asked.

wordCard.voice: Prophecy needs preparation. Maimonides' teaching that prophecy comes only to someone with a trained mind, a steady character and a strong imagination, and even then only as God gives it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: prophecy. Maimonides' term for what flows to a prepared mind and imagination.

carryVoice: Your line: prepare the vessel. Mind, character and imagination, made ready for whatever is given. Until tomorrow.
